title: Sustainability in numbers
heading: How far off is your gut?
intro: Eight real numbers about the environmental side of design: products, materials, waste and energy, in Germany, the UK and worldwide.
Every figure is real and sourced. Bet on how sure you are.

outro.heading: Design decides a lot.
paras: Many of today's numbers come back to decisions made long before a product reaches a shop: what it's made of, how long it's meant to last and what happens when it's thrown away.
Today you'll make some of those decisions. Use the evidence, and look carefully at the trade-offs.

questions.q: According to the European Commission, how much of a product's environmental impact is decided at the design stage?
questions.explain: The EU estimates that up to 80% of a product's environmental impact is decided during design, before anything is made. That's why EU ecodesign rules focus on designers, not only on recycling.
questions.source: European Parliament, circular economy press release, February 2021 (EU estimate)

questions.q: How much electronic waste did the world produce in 2022?
questions.explain: The world produced a record 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022, and the amount is growing about five times faster than documented recycling. Europeans produce the most per person, about 17.6 kg a year.

questions.q: Earth Overshoot Day is the date when humanity has used a year's worth of nature's resources. If everyone lived like people in Germany, when would it fall in 2025?
questions.explain: If everyone lived like the average German, the world would use up a year's resources by 3 May; we would need about three Earths. The global date in 2025 was 24 July, and Germany's 2026 date was 10 May.

questions.q: Roughly how much water does it take to make one cotton T-shirt?
questions.explain: Making one cotton T-shirt takes an estimated 2,700 litres of fresh water, mostly to grow the cotton: enough for one person to drink for about two and a half years.

questions.q: What share of global CO2 emissions comes from buildings and construction, counting both running buildings and making their materials?
questions.explain: Buildings and construction account for around 37% of global CO2 emissions: heating, cooling and powering buildings, plus making materials such as cement and steel. The sector also uses about 28% of the world's energy, so how buildings are designed is one of the biggest levers on climate.
questions.source: UNEP / GlobalABC, Global Status Report for Buildings and Construction 2025–2026, May 2026

questions.q: After England's 1990 World Cup penalty shoot-out on TV, millions of people in Britain switched on their kettles at once. How big was the jump in electricity demand?
questions.explain: Demand jumped by about 2,800 megawatts when the shoot-out ended, the biggest 'TV pickup' ever recorded in Britain, roughly a million kettles boiling at once. Grid engineers still plan for big TV moments.
questions.source: National Grid, reported by BBC News, 2007

questions.q: In 2023, before the UK banned single-use vapes in June 2025, roughly how many were thrown away each week?
questions.explain: About 5 million single-use vapes were thrown away every week in 2023, nearly four times the year before, each with a lithium battery inside. The estimate came from a YouGov survey; the government said the ban would cut litter and protect young people.

questions.q: How many disposable hot-drink cups are used in Germany every year?
questions.explain: An estimated 2.8 billion disposable cups a year, roughly 320,000 every hour; the figure is from a 2016 study and is still the one most quoted. Since 2023, larger cafés and takeaways must also offer a reusable option.
questions.source: Deutsche Umwelthilfe, based on an Umweltbundesamt study (2016 data); German Packaging Act (VerpackG) 2023
